title: Fixed-point acceleration on Neural Wasserstein manifolds
authors: Vitalii Aksenov, Sebastian Gutierrez Hernandez
abstract: We propose a fixed-point acceleration method for optimization over probability measures, applicable to a variety of machine learning problems. We represent probability measures as pushforwards of a reference distribution through a neural network map and equip the parameter space with the induced pullback Wasserstein metric. This geometric structure allows natural gradient descent to be interpreted as a fixed-point iteration on a Riemannian manifold. We accelerate this iteration using Riemannian Anderson mixing method, which exploits historical residuals to capture approximate second-order information without forming Hessians. In the present parametric setting, the manifold is represented by Euclidean coordinates endowed with a point-dependent metric, simplifying retraction and vector transport. We evaluate the method on multimodal sampling, PDE-based inverse problems, aggregation dynamics, Bayesian logistic regression, and generative modeling. Across the tested tasks, Anderson mixing reduces the number of natural-gradient iterations and achieves competitive performance relative to SGD and Adam in terms of both loss-gradient evaluations and wall-clock time. These results suggest that fixed-point acceleration is an efficient tool for improving the computational efficiency of training on parametric Wasserstein methods.

infographic.key_insight: Riemannian Anderson mixing accelerates natural-gradient optimization on neural Wasserstein manifolds by reusing past residuals without forming Hessians.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The method offers a way to reduce training iterations for probability-measure optimization in sampling, inverse problems, and generative modeling.
method: Represent probability measures as neural-network pushforwards of a reference distribution.
Equip network parameters with a pullback Wasserstein metric and interpret natural-gradient updates as fixed-point iterations.
Apply Riemannian Anderson mixing using historical residuals to capture approximate second-order information.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across multimodal sampling, PDE inverse problems, aggregation dynamics, Bayesian logistic regression, and generative modeling, the abstract reports fewer natural-gradient iterations and competitive gradient-evaluation counts and wall-clock time relative to SGD and Adam.
infographic.watch_item: Practical gains may depend on the cost and numerical stability of the point-dependent metric and residual-history computations.
infographic.paper_title: Fixed-point acceleration on Neural Wasserstein manifolds

title: Inverse design of superconductors and semiconductors with differentiable foundation models
authors: Cristóbal Méndez, Justin Tahmassebpur, Tomás A. Arias
abstract: Designing a crystal for a target property requires choosing its elements, stoichiometry, and atomic structure together, yet gradients exist only for the continuous structural variables. We introduce differentiable Equiformer fast effective-atom theory (DEFEAT), which lets a pretrained EquiformerV3 foundation model accept continuous species weights and site occupancies without retraining on fractional data, thereby enabling gradient-based materials optimization. Gradients from fine-tuned property models and a machine-learned energy penalty then guide updates to composition, atom count, atomic positions, and lattice vectors in a single optimization. In a search for phonon-mediated superconductors, density-functional perturbation theory on 45 structurally novel designs gives isotropic Allen-Dynes critical temperatures above 10 K for 39; the highest is 24.0 K for ZrTiNb2CN3, and H4LiPd3 (23.2 K) lies on the static DFT hull. In searches for photovoltaic absorbers, SCAN calculations confirm ten novel crystal structures with band gaps within 20% of a 1.34 eV target on their respective raw or empirically corrected scales, all within 70 meV/atom of the DFT hull, and show that the systematic gap error of the training functional propagates into the designs unless the objective corrects for it. Quasiharmonic free energies from machine-learned potentials further show that finite-temperature competition with solid phases can reorder candidates relative to the static hull.

infographic.key_insight: DEFEAT makes crystal composition and occupancy differentiable, enabling joint gradient-based optimization of elements, atom count, atomic positions, and lattice vectors.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The approach enables targeted searches for superconductors and photovoltaic absorbers while incorporating predicted properties and an energy penalty.
method: Extend pretrained EquiformerV3 to continuous species weights and site occupancies without fractional-data retraining.
Combine fine-tuned property-model gradients with a machine-learned energy penalty to optimize crystals.
Evaluate designs using first-principles calculations and assess finite-temperature phase competition with machine-learned potentials.
infographic.evidence_signal: DFPT evaluation found Allen–Dynes critical temperatures above 10 K for 39 of 45 structurally novel designs, peaking at 24.0 K; SCAN confirmed ten novel absorber structures within 20% of a 1.34 eV target on raw or corrected gap scales and within 70 meV/atom of the DFT hull.
infographic.watch_item: Training-functional band-gap bias can propagate into designs unless corrected in the objective, and finite-temperature phase competition can reorder static-hull rankings.
infographic.paper_title: Inverse design of superconductors and semiconductors with differentiable foundation models

title: Discovering formally verified quantum programs with AI
authors: Sergey Shirobokov, Ben Jaderberg, Katerina Hristova, George Tsoukalas, Johannes Bausch, Eric Wieser
abstract: The timeline by which quantum computers can solve breakthrough problems in science depends on improved quantum algorithms as much as on better hardware. Such algorithmic advances are typically achieved through many years of expert human collaboration. In mathematics and computer science, large language models have accelerated progress through automated discovery loops. However, quantum algorithms can only be evaluated by classical computers on restricted or small instances. Here we demonstrate automated discovery of quantum programs beyond these regimes including order-of-magnitude improvements on scientific applications. To achieve this, we build a quantum program library in the Lean theorem prover in which large language model agents synthesize novel programs against formal problem specifications and verify their correctness and cost. Agent teams collaborate, sharing results and knowledge through wikis and discussing ideas at organized conferences. Our results improve on prior baselines for parallel search (up to 1.4x), quantum arithmetic (290x), and simulations relevant to fusion, photochemistry and drug-metabolism by 11x, 8x and 2.5x respectively. Combining human and artificial intelligence at scale, under the rigor of mathematical proof, lets researchers design algorithms that today's classical and quantum computers cannot test, shortening the path to practical quantum computation.

infographic.key_insight: AI agents discovered quantum programs with formally verified correctness and cost, achieving substantial improvements over prior baselines.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Formal verification enables quantum algorithm development beyond classically testable regimes, potentially reducing resource requirements for scientific applications.
method: Build a quantum program library in the Lean theorem prover.
Have language-model agents synthesize programs against formal specifications and verify correctness and cost.
Coordinate agent teams through shared wikis and organized conferences.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports improvements over prior baselines of up to 1.4× for parallel search, 290× for quantum arithmetic, and 11×, 8× and 2.5× for simulations relevant to fusion, photochemistry and drug metabolism, respectively.
infographic.watch_item: Verified correctness and cost do not establish practical hardware speedups; deployment depends on physical implementation and resource overheads.
infographic.paper_title: Discovering formally verified quantum programs with AI

title: MemoryDojo: Benchmarking Poisoning Through LLM Agent Memory
authors: David H. Yang, Blake Bullwinkel, Amanda Minnich, Mohammad Mohammadi Amiri, Giorgio Severi
abstract: LLM agents benefit from using memory systems to improve performance on long-horizon, multi-session tasks. However, memory introduces a critical attack surface. Malicious instructions encountered in one session may be stored and propagated through memory before being retrieved and acted upon in later sessions. Because memory systems differ in how they process and retrieve information, the downstream effects of poisoning can vary significantly across systems. To quantify the effects of poisoning across different memory architectures, we introduce MemoryDojo, a benchmark for tracing the lifecycle of poisoned information through agent memory and measuring its influence on subsequent agent behavior. MemoryDojo is easily extensible, consists of 155 multi-session long-horizon trajectories covering four domains, and supports five different memory systems. Through our evaluation, we find that all memory systems are susceptible to memory poisoning, with substantial variation in downstream effects. We further propose a memory-aware poison optimization process that increases the poisoning efficacy, highlighting differences between memory architectures. We hope that MemoryDojo will support research on understanding and mitigating agentic memory risks.

infographic.key_insight: MemoryDojo shows that malicious instructions can persist through agent memory and influence later behavior, with all five evaluated memory systems susceptible.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Long-running research and engineering agents need safeguards against poisoned memories, not just malicious inputs in the current session.
method: Trace poisoned information across storage, retrieval, and subsequent agent behavior.
Benchmark five memory systems on multi-session, long-horizon tasks.
Use memory-aware poison optimization to increase attack efficacy.
infographic.evidence_signal: The benchmark includes 155 trajectories across four domains, and evaluation finds substantial variation in poisoning effects across memory systems.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract does not report numerical attack success rates, limiting quantitative comparison of memory architectures.
infographic.paper_title: MemoryDojo: Benchmarking Poisoning Through LLM Agent Memory

title: On the Reliability of Majority-Vote Pseudo-Labels in Test-Time Reinforcement Learning
authors: Haoyu Wang, Ru Wang, Yuanyuan Wang, Jiaxian Guo, Mingming Gong
abstract: Test-time reinforcement learning (TTRL) adapts pretrained language models to unlabeled target-domain data using self-generated pseudo-labels, whose reliability remains poorly understood. We analyze majority-vote supervision for TTRL with online Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) and decompose its error into population-majority bias and prompt-dependent finite-rollout variation. Because population-majority bias is generally unidentifiable without external supervision, we focus on mitigating the downstream effects of finite-rollout variation. We propose \emph{Prompt-Conditional Distributionally Robust DPO (PC-Dr.DPO)}, which conditions within-prompt robust reweighting on observed vote reliability to make updates from sampling-sensitive prompts more conservative. We further introduce a cache-based mechanism to reduce self-supervised forgetting during online adaptation. Across six mathematical and knowledge-intensive reasoning benchmarks and five model backbones, PC-Dr.DPO matches or outperforms the strongest TTRL baseline in 24 of 30 settings.

infographic.key_insight: PC-Dr.DPO makes test-time learning more conservative when majority-vote pseudo-labels are sensitive to finite sampling, without claiming to correct population-majority bias.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The approach targets more reliable adaptation of pretrained language models to unlabeled domains by moderating uncertain updates and reducing self-supervised forgetting.
method: Decompose majority-vote error into population-majority bias and prompt-dependent finite-rollout variation.
Condition within-prompt robust DPO reweighting on observed vote reliability.
Use a cache-based mechanism to reduce forgetting during online adaptation.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across six mathematical and knowledge-intensive reasoning benchmarks and five model backbones, PC-Dr.DPO matches or outperforms the strongest TTRL baseline in 24 of 30 settings.
infographic.watch_item: Population-majority bias is generally unidentifiable without external supervision, so stable majority votes can still yield incorrect pseudo-labels.
infographic.paper_title: On the Reliability of Majority-Vote Pseudo-Labels in Test-Time Reinforcement Learning

title: A Tight Hierarchy for Chain of Thought
authors: Thanh Le, A. Pavan, N. V. Vinodchandran
abstract: Chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning has emerged as a powerful paradigm for extending the computational capabilities of transformer-based models. A growing body of recent work has begun to uncover the fine-grained computational power of transformers augmented with CoT, as well as their connections to classical complexity theory. In this work, we advance this line of research by establishing the first hierarchy theorem for CoT-based computation. Our main result shows that for any reasonable resource bound $r(n) \geq n$ and any $\varepsilon > 0$, \[ \mathrm{CoT}(r(n)) \subsetneq \mathrm{CoT}(r(n)^{1+\varepsilon}), \] where $\mathrm{CoT}(r(n))$ denotes the class of decision problems solvable by transformers using $O(r(n))$ CoT reasoning steps on inputs of length $n$. Our result shows that increasing the number of CoT reasoning steps provably yields strictly greater computational power, establishing CoT steps as a fundamental resource in transformer-based computation. Unlike classical hierarchy theorems, which are typically proved via diagonalization, our approach leverages known coarse-grained simulations between CoT-augmented transformers and Turing machines in both directions. Building on these connections, we adapt the classical padding technique from complexity theory to this setting to obtain a tight hierarchy. A key technical contribution of our work is the implementation of padding within the transformer-based CoT model.

infographic.key_insight: For any reasonable resource bound r(n) ≥ n and any ε > 0, CoT(r(n)) ⊊ CoT(r(n)^(1+ε)), proving that more reasoning steps strictly expand transformer computational power.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The theorem establishes reasoning-step budgets as a computational resource, without guaranteeing better practical accuracy from longer reasoning.
method: Use known simulations between CoT-augmented transformers and Turing machines.
Adapt classical complexity-theoretic padding to establish a tight hierarchy.
Implement padding within the transformer-based CoT model.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports a formal hierarchy theorem, not dataset experiments or empirical model evaluations.
infographic.watch_item: The result concerns formal decision-problem classes; practical gains under finite context, precision, and compute budgets are not established in the abstract.
infographic.paper_title: A Tight Hierarchy for Chain of Thought

title: TensorMutation: Learning Weight-Space Mutations of Deep Learning Models on Neural Graphs
authors: Zaheed Ahmed, Philip Makedonski, Jens Grabowski
abstract: Mutation testing for deep learning (DL) faces a cost-realism trade-off. The pre-training approach produces realistic but computationally expensive mutants, whereas existing post-training operators modify trained models efficiently but produce mutants that less closely resemble real faults. This study asks whether the trade-off is necessary: can the weight-space effect of a fault-informed pre-training mutation operator be predicted from a trained model, without retraining it? We answer this question with TensorMutation, which represents a trained model as a neural graph and uses a mutation-conditioned graph neural network (GNN) to predict parameter changes. The GNN is trained offline and reused across unseen models so that TensorMutation can generate executable mutants without retraining. We construct a corpus of 25,252 original-mutant pairs from 71 multilayer perceptron (MLP) classifiers using 11 fault-informed pre-training operators, including 25 newly curated subjects. TensorMutation partially reproduces the behavioral effects of pre-training mutations on nine held-out subjects, and direct weight-space supervision significantly improves weight-space fidelity. On 12 real-fault subjects, TensorMutation achieves the highest median behavioral similarity among the evaluated approaches. The improvement over the post-training tool DeepMutation++ is statistically significant (Holm-adjusted p=0.018), whereas the differences from the pre-training tool DeepCrime and the norm-matched random control are not significant. These results show that fault-informed pre-training mutations leave learnable structure in weight space that transfers to unseen models.

infographic.key_insight: TensorMutation learns transferable weight-space effects of fault-informed training mutations, enabling mutant generation without retraining each model.
infographic.engineering_relevance: A reusable mutation predictor could reduce the computational cost of deep-learning mutation testing while approximating realistic training faults.
method: Represent a trained model as a neural graph.
Use a mutation-conditioned GNN to predict parameter changes.
Train offline on original–mutant pairs and reuse across unseen models.
infographic.evidence_signal: Using 25,252 pairs from 71 MLP classifiers and 11 mutation operators, TensorMutation partially reproduced mutation behavior on nine held-out subjects and achieved the highest median behavioral similarity on 12 real-fault subjects.
infographic.watch_item: Evidence is limited to MLP classifiers; real-fault similarity improved significantly over DeepMutation++ but not over DeepCrime or a norm-matched random control.
infographic.paper_title: TensorMutation: Learning Weight-Space Mutations of Deep Learning Models on Neural Graphs

title: BiLoGo: Reducing the smoothing of localised responses in Transformer-based neural operators for sheet forming
authors: Yingxue Zhao, Haoran Li, Haosu Zhou, Tobias Pfaff, Nan Li
abstract: Trial-and-error FE simulation of sheet forming could be computationally expensive, neural-network-based learned simulators are used to accelerate design. These simulators should accurately capture localised responses, such as thinning around sharp radii or near ribs, which determine formability. Transformer-based neural operators propagate information efficiently across the mesh but tend to smooth such localised responses. This study develops BiLoGo, a Bipartite Local-Global learned simulator with an FE-guided design that connects local node-element message passing with a Transformer-based neural operator for long-range information exchange. BiLoGo has three modules: a bidirectional node-element GraphSAGE model that learns nodal-elemental coupling on a bipartite graph and predicts each quantity on its native FE entity without interpolation; a dual-stream Transformer-based neural operator that processes blank deformation and tool contact with separate token sets, preventing localised contact information from being averaged with the whole-blank state; and a fusion and element update module that combines global and local features via gated residual fusion and updates element features conditioned on element-node kinematics. Evaluated on a dome-shaped cold forming case and two corner-shaped hot stamping cases (one with ribs), BiLoGo achieves the lowest positional and threshold-based thinning errors on all three cases compared with single-level and hierarchical graph-based models and Transformer-based neural operators. Near the ribs, the smoothing index of predicted thinning increases from 0.41-0.56 for Transformer-based neural operators to 0.94 for BiLoGo-U. Compared with the hierarchical graph network CAtt-BiUGNN, BiLoGo-T reduces mean positional error by 15.5% on the Corner case and BiLoGo-U by 8.3% on the Corner+Rib case, with 66-69% less training memory.

infographic.key_insight: BiLoGo combines local FE-mesh learning with global Transformer communication to reduce smoothing of critical, localised sheet-forming responses.
infographic.engineering_relevance: More accurate localisation of thinning near ribs and sharp radii could improve learned simulators used to accelerate sheet-forming design.
method: Bidirectional node–element GraphSAGE predicts quantities on their native FE entities without interpolation.
Dual-stream Transformer tokens separate blank deformation from tool contact information.
Gated residual fusion combines local and global features, with element updates conditioned on element–node kinematics.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across three forming cases, BiLoGo achieved the lowest positional and threshold-based thinning errors among tested models; near ribs, BiLoGo-U raised the thinning smoothing index to 0.94 versus 0.41–0.56 for Transformer baselines.
infographic.watch_item: Evaluation covers three forming cases; generalisation to broader geometries, materials and process conditions remains to be established.
infographic.paper_title: BiLoGo: Reducing the smoothing of localised responses in Transformer-based neural operators for sheet forming

title: Solver-Free Decision-Focused Learning via Neural Optimization Layers for Edge Selection
authors: Xinda Zheng, Frits de Nijs, Edward Lam
abstract: Decision-focused learning trains prediction models to improve downstream decisions, but many methods require costly solver calls or optimal-solution labels. We propose a solver-free decision-focused learning framework for NP-hard edge-selection problems with uncertain parameters in the objective, the constraints, or both. A neural optimization layer is first trained without solution labels, using problem objectives and constraint penalties. Graph-informed edge scoring and iterative refinement encourage concentrated and structurally consistent continuous decisions. The layer is then frozen, and a prediction model is trained through its continuous output using a problem-specific loss evaluated under observed parameters. At deployment, the predictor, optimization layer, and a lightweight decoder produce decisions without solving the original NP-hard problem. Experiments on the asymmetric traveling salesperson and endpoint-free orienteering problems show consistently better decision quality than prediction-focused learning and improvements over most evaluated decision-focused baselines. Our framework requires less training time than the evaluated decision-focused baselines, even when optimization-layer pretraining is included. Neural deployment also produces decisions faster than solver-based deployment, offering a better quality-efficiency trade-off. The layer also reduces training cost in existing decision-focused methods when used as an approximate optimization oracle.

infographic.key_insight: A pretrained neural optimization layer enables solver-free decision-focused learning for NP-hard edge-selection problems without optimal-solution labels.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The framework offers a quality–efficiency trade-off for routing decisions by reducing training cost and avoiding NP-hard solver calls at deployment.
method: Pretrain a neural optimization layer using objectives and constraint penalties, with graph-informed edge scoring and iterative refinement.
Freeze the layer and train a predictor through continuous decisions using a task-specific loss evaluated under observed parameters.
Deploy the predictor, optimization layer, and lightweight decoder to produce discrete decisions.
infographic.evidence_signal: On asymmetric traveling salesperson and endpoint-free orienteering tasks, the framework outperformed prediction-focused learning and most evaluated decision-focused baselines, with lower training time and faster deployment than solver-based approaches.
infographic.watch_item: Constraint penalties and lightweight decoding do not establish a general feasibility or optimality guarantee; validate decoded decisions under deployment conditions.
infographic.paper_title: Solver-Free Decision-Focused Learning via Neural Optimization Layers for Edge Selection

title: Scaling Graph Similarity Learning with Graph Neural Networks
authors: Ahmet Tüzen, Helge Langseth, Kjetil Nørvåg
abstract: Graph similarity computation is an important task in graph mining with many real-world applications, such as chemical compound analysis, program dependence comparison, and social network analysis. The problem is computationally challenging: Graph Edit Distance (GED) and Maximum Common Subgraph (MCS), which quantify the distance between graphs and identify their largest shared subgraph, respectively, are NP-hard to compute exactly. To address these computational challenges, Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have been applied to this problem. However, existing GNN-based approaches have primarily focused on small-scale graph datasets, while scalability to larger scales remains underexplored. In this work, we propose FiLSim, a scalable GNN-based framework, and investigate whether a simplified GNN pipeline can maintain competitive performance on standard benchmarks while scaling to large graphs. We additionally propose a sequential graph-editing strategy to construct large-scale graph datasets with reliable GED labels to evaluate scalability. The proposed framework is evaluated on four benchmark datasets and four newly created large-scale datasets, demonstrating its effectiveness and scalability. FiLSim remains accurate on graphs with more than 150{,}000 nodes, where the baseline methods run out of memory or fail to learn, and scores all test pairs within seconds on a single GPU.

infographic.key_insight: FiLSim uses a simplified GNN pipeline to learn graph similarity accurately at scales exceeding 150,000 nodes.
infographic.engineering_relevance: FiLSim offers a scalable learned alternative to computationally expensive exact graph similarity calculations, scoring all evaluated test pairs within seconds on a single GPU.
method: Use a simplified GNN-based framework for graph similarity learning.
Construct large-scale datasets through sequential graph editing with reliable graph edit distance labels.
Evaluate prediction performance and scalability against baseline methods.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across four benchmark and four newly created large-scale datasets, FiLSim remained accurate on graphs exceeding 150,000 nodes, where baselines ran out of memory or failed to learn.
infographic.watch_item: Performance on edit-generated datasets may not fully predict generalization to naturally occurring large graphs; hardware and workload details are needed to interpret runtime claims.
infographic.paper_title: Scaling Graph Similarity Learning with Graph Neural Networks

title: Steerable Multi-Objective Group-Relative Preference Optimization with Jointly Trained Low-Rank Adapters
authors: Constantinos Karouzos, Nikolaos Aletras
abstract: Language model deployment often requires different trade-offs between competing objectives as user preferences change, yet standard post-training methods typically produce a single policy for a fixed objective weighting. We introduce LambdaMix, a new parameter efficient method for learning a preference conditioned family of policies with group-relative online reinforcement learning. LambdaMix jointly trains one low-rank adapter per objective over a frozen base model. One preference vector selects the adapter mixture that generates responses and weights the separately normalized rewards used to update the adapters. A single training run supports changing preferences at inference without further optimization. We experiment with four models on helpfulness and harmlessness and on solving math problems while following instructions. We also evaluate the two largest models on rewriting comments to preserve wording while reducing clues about personal attributes. On the first two tasks, LambdaMix achieves higher hypervolume than all evaluated conditioned and policy merging baselines across all four models. LambdaMix uses fewer training completions and stores fewer adapter parameters than a set of GRPO specialist policies. With architecture and initialization fixed, varying adapter mixtures and objective weights together gives wider score ranges and higher coverage than varying either alone.

infographic.key_insight: LambdaMix learns a family of preference-conditioned language model policies in one training run, enabling inference-time trade-offs without further optimization.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Teams can adapt deployed model behavior to changing priorities using jointly trained low-rank adapters rather than maintaining separate specialist policies.
method: Freeze the base model and jointly train one low-rank adapter per objective with group-relative online reinforcement learning.
Use one preference vector to select the adapter mixture and weight separately normalized objective rewards.
Change the preference vector at inference to steer objective trade-offs.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across four models on helpfulness–harmlessness and math–instruction-following tasks, LambdaMix achieved higher hypervolume than all evaluated conditioned and policy-merging baselines while using fewer training completions and stored adapter parameters than GRPO specialists.
infographic.watch_item: Results cover a limited set of objectives and models; performance with more objectives or under deployment distribution shifts remains unestablished.
infographic.paper_title: Steerable Multi-Objective Group-Relative Preference Optimization with Jointly Trained Low-Rank Adapters

title: CPU-ARC: Agentic Reasoning Caching for on-CPU Reasoning Reuse
authors: Peter Belcak, Greg Heinrich, Saurav Muralidharan, Shizhe Diao, Pavlo Molchanov
abstract: Large language models reinvent the wheel all the time. They conflate task-solving with the execution of the solutions, which forces them to solve every problem from scratch. We show that once a task has been reasoned through, the application of its solution to a new problem instance can be done very efficiently and with little involvement from language models. We introduce agentic reasoning caching, a method for constructing robust CPU-executable agentic reasoning caches (ARCs) from LLM reasoning traces. ARCs show on-par performance with frontier LLMs across a range of difficult mathematical and scientific tasks, are fully explainable, continually trainable, robust to input perturbations, and 16-291x cheaper to invoke than the source model.

infographic.key_insight: CPU-ARC turns LLM reasoning traces into reusable CPU-executable caches, separating solution discovery from execution on new problem instances.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Reusing executable reasoning could reduce repeated LLM calls and inference costs in mathematical and scientific workflows.
method: Construct agentic reasoning caches (ARCs) from LLM reasoning traces.
Execute cached solutions on CPUs for new problem instances with little LLM involvement.
Support explainable, continually trainable reasoning reuse.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports performance on par with frontier LLMs across difficult mathematical and scientific tasks, robustness to input perturbations, and 16–291× cheaper invocation than the source model.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract does not quantify cache-construction costs or define when a new instance falls outside a cache’s valid scope.
infographic.paper_title: CPU-ARC: Agentic Reasoning Caching for on-CPU Reasoning Reuse

title: Designing Effective Monitor-Based Interventions for Mitigating Reward Hacking During RL
authors: Aria Wong, Joshua Engels, Neel Nanda
abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) rewards are notoriously difficult to design and control, often leading to the model learning unintended behaviors such as reward hacking. One potential solution is to monitor for reward hacking and penalize it when detected; however, training against a monitor could lead to evasive behavior, and our general understanding of how to apply monitors effectively during training is limited. To study how best to use monitors to mitigate reward hacking, we introduce and open source three realistic environments where Qwen3-4B reward hacks: a coding environment hackable via test overwriting, a medical chat environment hackable via sycophancy, and a biography generation environment hackable via hallucination. We first focus on the coding environment, where we find that: (1) models can learn to evade highly accurate monitors by exploiting systemic flaws in probes and LLM judges; (2) monitors that leak more learning signal during RL suppress reward hacking but are more often evaded; and (3) including easier problems in training can decrease reward hacking. We apply our findings to build better reward hacking monitors for the medical chat and biography generation environments that improve upon naive baselines to reduce reward hacking rates across seeds to before-training levels in some interventions. Our results demonstrate that our takeaways translate to new settings and that better monitor intervention designs are possible.

infographic.key_insight: Monitor-based penalties can reduce reward hacking during RL, but models may learn to evade even highly accurate monitors.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Effective monitoring requires intervention design beyond detection accuracy, including careful feedback signals and training-task difficulty.
method: Introduce three open-source Qwen3-4B environments: coding test overwriting, medical sycophancy, and biography hallucination.
Study monitor evasion, learning-signal exposure, and easier training problems in the coding environment.
Apply the findings to improve monitors in medical chat and biography generation.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across seeds, some interventions reduced reward hacking to pre-training levels in the medical chat and biography environments, improving on naive baselines.
infographic.watch_item: Monitors that expose more learning signal can suppress hacking yet invite evasion; results from Qwen3-4B may not generalize to other models.
infographic.paper_title: Designing Effective Monitor-Based Interventions for Mitigating Reward Hacking During RL

title: Attend at the Right Resolution: Head-Adaptive Sparse Attention via Query-Key Interaction Structure
authors: Wajih Hassan Raza, Ahsan Bilal, Yidan Shen, Renjie Hu, Xin Fu, Yu Wen
abstract: Attention is a major scalability bottleneck in large language models (LLMs), with its computational cost and key-value (KV) memory traffic becoming increasingly prohibitive as context length grows. Sparse attention addresses this bottleneck by restricting each query to a subset of the context, but its effectiveness hinges on identifying relevant regions both cheaply and reliably. Existing training-free methods primarily rely on runtime relevance estimates, with selection dimensionality and granularity typically governed by fixed heuristics rather than the intrinsic interaction structure of pretrained attention heads. We take a different perspective: the query-key operator of each pretrained head defines a characteristic response structure that determines the resolution needed for sparse selection, both across feature directions and across context tokens. Building on this insight, we propose Head-Adaptive Sparse Attention (HASA), a training-free sparse attention framework that jointly adapts selection resolution along these two dimensions. Along the feature dimension, the singular spectrum of each head's query-key operator determines an effective rank, yielding a compact, head-specific response space. Along the sequence dimension, neighboring regions are progressively merged according to the directional coherence of their token responses in this same space, while heterogeneous regions remain separate. Exact attention is then computed using the original full-dimensional KV states of the selected regions. HASA captures 88.1% of dense-attention mass and, compared with UNIQUE, a strong recent sparse-attention baseline, improves accuracy by up to 3.47 and 2.57 points on RULER and LongBench-Pro, respectively, and accelerates self-attention by up to 1.32x, while achieving up to 14.07x speedup over dense attention.

infographic.key_insight: HASA uses each pretrained attention head’s query-key interaction structure to adapt sparse selection across both feature directions and context regions.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This training-free approach targets long-context inference costs by selecting relevant regions cheaply before computing exact attention with their original full-dimensional KV states.
method: Derive a head-specific compact response space from the query-key operator’s singular spectrum.
Progressively merge neighboring context regions with directionally coherent responses, keeping heterogeneous regions separate.
Select regions in the compact space, then compute exact attention using their full-dimensional KV states.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports 88.1% dense-attention mass capture, accuracy gains over UNIQUE of up to 3.47 points on RULER and 2.57 on LongBench-Pro, and self-attention speedups up to 1.32× over UNIQUE and 14.07× over dense attention.
infographic.watch_item: Reported speedups concern self-attention rather than end-to-end inference; practical gains should be checked against selection overhead and deployment hardware.
infographic.paper_title: Attend at the Right Resolution: Head-Adaptive Sparse Attention via Query-Key Interaction Structure

title: A Generalized Bayesian Approach to Clustering with Dimension Reduction
authors: Shen Jia, Weipeng Huang, Geng Yang, Eoin Gallagher, Tin Lok James Ng
abstract: Generalized Bayes product partition models provide a probabilistic counterpart to loss-based clustering. They update a prior over partitions through an exponentiated clustering loss rather than a likelihood, so allocation uncertainty can be quantified without a full generative model for the data. However, their performance depends on the space in which the loss is evaluated. For high-dimensional observations, a squared Euclidean loss on the raw features can be dominated by irrelevant coordinates or fail to reflect cluster structure lying near a nonlinear low-dimensional manifold. We propose an extension in which an autoencoder and the partition are learned together, so that the space in which the clustering loss is evaluated is shaped by the clustering itself. Our generalized posterior combines a reconstruction loss, which keeps the low-dimensional representation faithful to the observed data, with a within-cluster sum of squares in the latent representation, which encourages cluster separation. Posterior computation alternates between Gibbs sampling over partitions and gradient-based updates of the autoencoder network, with the learning rate estimated jointly. We illustrate the approach through simulation studies and applications to four benchmark datasets.

infographic.key_insight: Jointly learning an autoencoder and a generalized Bayesian partition lets clustering shape its latent space while quantifying allocation uncertainty without a full generative data model.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The approach targets high-dimensional data where irrelevant features or nonlinear structure can undermine clustering based on raw Euclidean distances.
method: Update a partition prior using exponentiated losses rather than a likelihood.
Combine autoencoder reconstruction loss with latent-space within-cluster sum of squares.
Alternate Gibbs sampling of partitions with gradient-based network updates, jointly estimating the learning rate.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports simulation studies and applications to four benchmark datasets, but provides no quantitative performance results.
infographic.watch_item: Alternating partition sampling and neural-network optimization warrants checks for convergence and sensitivity to initialization.
infographic.paper_title: A Generalized Bayesian Approach to Clustering with Dimension Reduction

title: Autonomous Particle Image Velocimetry Using Zero-Shot Sim-to-Real Reinforcement Learning
authors: Chang Rajani, Luke Sebastien Marsden, Stephan Kunz, Claudio Mucignat, Ivan Lunati
abstract: Particle image velocimetry (PIV) reconstructs a flow field from the motion of tracer particles but the reconstruction quality is bounded by how well the flow structure of interest is resolved in the images. The acquisition position is typically fixed by the operator before the measurement. We cast camera placement as a sequential decision-making problem and train a reinforcement learning agent to control a 6-DoF manipulator equipped with a camera, enabling it to locate, frame and resolve a hydrofoil wake in a water tunnel. The agent commands the camera pose and observes the scene only through the velocity field and uncertainty estimated from time-separated image pairs. It is trained entirely in a photorealistic simulation of our water tunnel, with wakes generated by Computational Fluid Dynamics (CFD) simulations of hydrofoils with varying profiles, positions and angles of attack. After zero-shot transfer to the real water tunnel, the policy reliably locates and frames the wakes of randomly placed hydrofoils. It resolves the wake at a higher resolution than a fixed camera view and with lower error in the measured flow statistics, in roughly half the time of a full scan and with far fewer image pairs.

infographic.key_insight: A reinforcement learning agent trained entirely in simulation autonomously positions a PIV camera to locate and resolve hydrofoil wakes after zero-shot transfer to a real water tunnel.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Adaptive camera placement can improve flow-measurement resolution and accuracy while reducing acquisition time and image requirements.
method: Formulate camera placement as sequential control of a camera-equipped 6-DoF manipulator.
Use PIV-estimated velocity fields and uncertainty as the agent’s scene observations.
Train in a photorealistic water-tunnel simulation using CFD wakes spanning hydrofoil profiles, positions and angles of attack.
infographic.evidence_signal: Real-water-tunnel tests with randomly placed hydrofoils showed reliable wake framing, higher resolution and lower flow-statistics error than a fixed view, using roughly half the time of a full scan and far fewer image pairs.
infographic.watch_item: Transfer beyond the tested water-tunnel setup remains unestablished in the abstract and may depend on simulation fidelity and PIV uncertainty estimation.
infographic.paper_title: Autonomous Particle Image Velocimetry Using Zero-Shot Sim-to-Real Reinforcement Learning

title: Diffusion-free Score Matching for Exact Conditional Sampling
authors: Thomas Wedenig, Robert Peharz
abstract: The success of modern score-based generative models is largely driven by diffusion-based training, which learns a collection of time-indexed score fields corresponding to progressively noisier versions of the data distribution. While such models achieve impressive sample quality, leveraging them for sound probabilistic inference---particularly sampling from arbitrary conditionals of the model---remains challenging. This difficulty arises because conditioning information is only available for clean data and not for the higher noise levels required to generate exact conditional samples. In this paper, we introduce DIffusion-free SCOre matching (DISCO), a principled approach that sidesteps the need for time-dependent score fields altogether. Our method is based on an objective that, while reminiscent of diffusion-based training, estimates only a single score of the (slightly perturbed) data distribution, for which the exact conditional score is readily obtained. In experiments, DISCO is competitive with state-of-the-art diffusion models in terms of sample quality. More importantly, DISCO yields a more faithful representation of the underlying data distribution and---crucially---enables accurate sampling from arbitrary conditionals, outperforming standard heuristic samplers. This capability opens the door to principled and flexible probabilistic reasoning with score-based models.

infographic.key_insight: DISCO learns a single score field instead of time-indexed diffusion scores, enabling exact conditional scores for arbitrary observed subsets of the slightly perturbed data distribution.
infographic.engineering_relevance: DISCO could support flexible conditional generation and probabilistic inference without diffusion-specific conditioning heuristics.
method: Use diffusion-free score matching to estimate one score field for slightly perturbed data.
Obtain conditional scores directly from the learned joint score.
Use these scores to sample unobserved variables given arbitrary observed subsets.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports competitive sample quality versus state-of-the-art diffusion models, more faithful distribution modeling, and more accurate conditional sampling than standard heuristic samplers, but provides no datasets or numerical results.
infographic.watch_item: Exact conditional-score identities do not eliminate learned-score error, data-perturbation effects, or numerical sampling error.
infographic.paper_title: Diffusion-free Score Matching for Exact Conditional Sampling

title: FlowMoP: Stochastic Multi-Person Motion Prediction
authors: Aadya Agrawal, Ho Kei Cheng, Alexander Schwing
abstract: Predicting the future motion of multiple people is inherently stochastic: the same observed history admits many plausible continuations depending on intent, coordination, and social context. Yet the dominant paradigm in multi-person 3D motion prediction remains deterministic, with existing methods producing a fixed number of outputs per agent. In contrast, we present a conditional flow matching framework that jointly generates diverse future motions for multiple agents, modeling both global trajectories and root-relative poses. A B-spline reparameterization compresses the generative state space while enforcing temporal smoothness, and a dual-stream transformer conditions each agent's predictions on observed neighbor motion for interaction-aware forecasting. Our method achieves state-of-the-art performance on CMU-Mocap (UMPM) and 3DPW, outperforming deterministic baselines on joint position error, pose error, and final displacement error despite producing a full predictive distribution. We additionally establish the first motion prediction baseline on WorldPose, a large-scale professional soccer dataset, where social conditioning demonstrably concentrates predictive uncertainty along interaction-constrained directions.

infographic.key_insight: FlowMoP jointly predicts diverse, socially conditioned 3D motion futures for multiple people rather than a single deterministic continuation.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Distributional motion forecasts can support uncertainty-aware planning in systems that interact with moving people.
method: Conditional flow matching generates joint futures for global trajectories and root-relative poses.
B-spline reparameterization compresses the generative state and enforces temporal smoothness.
A dual-stream transformer conditions predictions on observed neighbor motion.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports state-of-the-art joint position, pose, and final displacement errors on CMU-Mocap (UMPM) and 3DPW, plus the first motion prediction baseline on WorldPose soccer data.
infographic.watch_item: Real-time sampling cost and uncertainty calibration are not established by the abstract.
infographic.paper_title: FlowMoP: Stochastic Multi-Person Motion Prediction

title: One Run Is Not Enough: A Monte Carlo Protocol for Evaluating LLM Reliability on Data Science Tasks
authors: Wenqi Ni, Ozan Evkaya, Miguel de Carvalho
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have shown promise for automating data science workflows. Benchmarks such as DataSciBench (2026) and StatQA (2024) have advanced the evaluation of their capabilities across data science and statistical tasks. Assessing their reliability requires examining both the quality of their responses and their consistency across repeated runs, task types, and difficulty levels. With this aim, we introduce DS-QA, a benchmark comprising 100 data science and statistics questions drawn from UK university courses, spanning 16 datasets and three difficulty levels. We develop a three-layer evaluation framework that combines general response properties (runtime, verbosity and text similarity), coarse-grained metrics (accuracy, code executability and completeness), and task-specific metrics. We evaluate OpenAI models using a Monte Carlo protocol with 100 repeated runs. The results reveal substantial variability in responses to data visualisation and supervised learning tasks, particularly at medium and hard difficulty levels, highlighting the importance of evaluating consistency alongside response quality. We also find that an increase of 0.1 in the word verbosity ratio corresponds to an increase of about 0.013 in the token verbosity ratio.

infographic.key_insight: Repeated evaluation reveals substantial LLM response variability in data visualisation and supervised learning, especially on medium and hard tasks.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Evaluate data science assistants across repeated runs to measure consistency alongside answer quality before deployment.
method: Introduce DS-QA: 100 university-level questions spanning 16 datasets and three difficulty levels.
Assess general response properties, coarse-grained quality metrics and task-specific metrics.
Evaluate OpenAI models using a Monte Carlo protocol with 100 repeated runs.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across DS-QA evaluations, responses varied substantially by task and difficulty; a 0.1 increase in word verbosity ratio corresponded to about 0.013 higher token verbosity ratio.
infographic.watch_item: Findings from OpenAI models and university-course questions may not generalise to other models or production workflows.
infographic.paper_title: One Run Is Not Enough: A Monte Carlo Protocol for Evaluating LLM Reliability on Data Science Tasks

title: Encoding Memory in World Models with Test-Time Model-Based Reinforcement Learning
authors: Maxime Burchi, Fayaz Ali Dharejo, Radu Timofte
abstract: Model-based reinforcement learning (MBRL) approaches have demonstrated strong performance across diverse domains in recent years, learning accurate world models from agent trajectories. However, despite this progress, current approaches still struggle to surpass human performance on tasks that require long-term memory and planning. In this work, we address the problem of long-term memory in MBRL by moving beyond the commonly studied paradigm of architecture design. We introduce Test-Time Model-Based Reinforcement Learning (TT-MBRL), using gradient descent at test time to encode the memory of episode observations into world model parameters. This enables the agent to learn a distinct world model for each episode, improving memory capabilities compared to traditional approaches that solely rely on contextual memory. We first establish a proof of concept on a simplified two-dimensional variant of the Memory Maze environment, which we refer to as Memory Maze 2D, showing consistent improvements across different world model architectures. We then demonstrate the effectiveness of TT-MBRL in the 3D domain, achieving new state-of-the-art results on the Memory Maze benchmark. Finally, we show that TT-MBRL maintains strong performance on non-memory benchmarks such as DeepMind Control and Atari 100k.

infographic.key_insight: Test-time gradient updates encode episode observations into world model parameters, improving long-term memory beyond contextual memory alone.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Episode-specific world model adaptation could help reinforcement learning agents solve tasks requiring persistent memory and planning.
method: Update world model parameters with gradient descent at test time.
Encode observation history into a distinct world model for each episode.
Evaluate across memory-focused tasks and broader control benchmarks.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports consistent gains across world model architectures on Memory Maze 2D, new state-of-the-art results on 3D Memory Maze, and strong performance on DeepMind Control and Atari 100k.
infographic.watch_item: Test-time optimization introduces additional computation; the abstract does not quantify its latency or resource costs.
infographic.paper_title: Encoding Memory in World Models with Test-Time Model-Based Reinforcement Learning
